lead: Switch a DC source onto a circuit with one capacitor or one inductor and every voltage and current moves from its starting value to its final value with the same time constant τ; some rise, some fall. Each answer is the sum of a forced part set by the source and a natural part set by the mismatch at the switching instant. Engineers use this split to size a delay, read a datasheet or explain why a relay drops out late. This chapter shows the split, the one-line formula that joins the start and end values, and the sketch that follows from it.
prereq: You need: source-free circuits for τ and the decaying exponential, and KVL and KCL from circuit elements and laws.

blocks.text: A first-order circuit has one storage element, so after switching it obeys a first-order differential equation whose solution has two pieces. The forced (particular, steady-state) response follows the source. The natural (homogeneous, transient) response solves the equation with the source set to zero and always has the form A e<sup>−t/τ</sup>. The complete response is their sum:

items: For a series RL circuit, KVL for t > 0 gives L di/dt + R i = V<sub>s</sub>.
Natural part: set the source to zero, L di/dt + R i = 0, whose solution is i<sub>n</sub> = A e<sup>−Rt/L</sup> = A e<sup>−t/τ</sup> with τ = L/R.
Forced part: a constant source forces a constant current; put di/dt = 0 to get i<sub>f</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>/R.
Complete response: i = V<sub>s</sub>/R + A e<sup>−t/τ</sup>. The initial current fixes A: A = i(0⁺) − V<sub>s</sub>/R.

blocks.text: For a constant DC source, the forced response is simply the final value x(∞), because after the exponential dies nothing changes. The natural part must carry the difference between the initial value x(0⁺) and that final value. Hence the shortcut:

blocks.where: x is any current or voltage for t ≥ 0⁺; τ = R<sub>eq</sub>C or L/R<sub>eq</sub>, with R<sub>eq</sub> the resistance seen by the storage element with independent sources killed.

blocks.text: At t = 0⁺ the exponential is 1 and the formula gives x(0⁺); as t → ∞ it gives x(∞). The bracket is the initial mismatch, and if it is zero nothing moves.
For a series RC circuit with a DC voltage V<sub>s</sub> switched on at t = 0, KVL gives V<sub>s</sub> = R i + v<sub>C</sub> and i = C dv<sub>C</sub>/dt. With τ = RC,
vC(t) = Vs + [vC(0⁺) − Vs] e−t/τ, i(t) = [(Vs − vC(0⁺))/R] e−t/τ

For an uncharged capacitor, v<sub>C</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>(1 − e<sup>−t/τ</sup>) and i = (V<sub>s</sub>/R)e<sup>−t/τ</sup>. The capacitor voltage cannot jump, but its current can: it jumps to (V<sub>s</sub> − v<sub>C</sub>(0⁺))/R at t = 0⁺ and decays to 0.
For a series RL circuit driven by V<sub>s</sub>, KVL gives V<sub>s</sub> = R i + L di/dt. With τ = L/R,

I∞ is the final current. The inductor voltage can jump: v<sub>L</sub>(t) = [V<sub>s</sub> − R i(0⁺)] e<sup>−t/τ</sup>. For zero initial current, i = (V<sub>s</sub>/R)(1 − e<sup>−t/τ</sup>) and v<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>e<sup>−t/τ</sup>.

To sketch any first-order answer, mark x(0⁺) and x(∞) on the vertical axis. Draw an exponential from the first to the second. If x(∞) > x(0⁺), the curve rises; if x(∞) < x(0⁺), it falls. The initial slope is:

blocks.where: positive for a rising answer, negative for a falling one. The tangent at t = 0 reaches the final value at t = τ; after 5τ about 0.7 % of the mismatch is left.

blocks.text: A pulse is two steps in the same circuit. First the source switches on at t = 0 and the answer runs toward its on-state final value. At t = T<sub>p</sub> it switches off, and the same formula restarts with x(T<sub>p</sub>⁺) as the new initial value and a new final value, often zero. If T<sub>p</sub> is much larger than τ, the capacitor or inductor fully charges and then fully discharges; if T<sub>p</sub> is much smaller than τ, the capacitor voltage barely moves, so almost the whole pulse appears across the resistor: v<sub>R</sub> is a near copy of the pulse and v<sub>C</sub> a small rounded ramp. A repeating pulse train builds or droops according to this ratio.
With two storage elements the single exponential becomes two exponentials or a damped sine; see second-order RLC circuits.

figure.caption: The worked example split into its parts: the forced part is the flat 10 V, the natural part −10e⁻¹⁰ᵗ V starts at −10 V and dies away, and their sum, the capacitor voltage, starts at 0 V and reaches 6.32 V at t = τ = 0.1 s.

spec.aria: Plot from 0 to 0.5 seconds of the forced part 10 volts, the natural part minus 10 e to the minus 10 t, and their sum 10 times 1 minus e to the minus 10 t, which passes 6.32 volts at 0.1 seconds.

examples.question: A 10 V DC source is switched at t = 0 across a series combination of R = 50 kΩ and C = 2 μF. The capacitor is uncharged before switching. Find τ, v<sub>C</sub>(t), i(t), and v<sub>C</sub> at t = 0.1 s.
steps: For an uncharged capacitor, v<sub>C</sub>(0⁺) = 0 V. After the transient, the capacitor is open to DC, so v<sub>C</sub>(∞) = 10 V.
Use v<sub>C</sub>(t) = v<sub>C</sub>(∞) + [v<sub>C</sub>(0⁺) − v<sub>C</sub>(∞)] e<sup>−t/τ</sup> = 10 + (0 − 10)e<sup>−10t</sup> = 10(1 − e<sup>−10t</sup>) V.
i(t) = C dv<sub>C</sub>/dt = (2 × 10⁻⁶)(10)(10)e<sup>−10t</sup> A = 2 × 10⁻⁴ e<sup>−10t</sup> A = 0.2 e<sup>−10t</sup> mA.
examples.answer: τ = 0.1 s, v<sub>C</sub>(t) = 10(1 − e<sup>−10t</sup>) V, i(t) = 0.2 e<sup>−10t</sup> mA, and v<sub>C</sub>(0.1 s) = 6.32 V.
examples.check:
import math
R = 50e3
C = 2e-6
Vs = 10.0
tau = R * C
vC_inf = Vs
vC_0 = 0.0
i0_mA = (Vs - vC_0) / R * 1000
t = 0.1
vC_t = vC_inf + (vC_0 - vC_inf) * math.exp(-t / tau)
print(round(tau, 3))
print(vC_inf)
print(vC_0)
print(round(i0_mA, 3))
print(round(vC_t, 2))

examples.question: For a long time a 12 V source has driven R₁ = 4 Ω, R₂ = 2 Ω and L = 0.6 H in series. At t = 0 a switch shorts R₂. Find i(t) and v<sub>L</sub>(t) for t ≥ 0, name the forced and natural parts, and find when the current reaches 2.9 A.
steps: Before the switch the inductor is a short: i(0⁻) = 12/(4 + 2) = 2 A, and continuity gives i(0⁺) = 2 A.
After the switch only R₁ remains: i(∞) = 12/4 = 3 A and τ = L/R₁ = 0.6/4 = 0.15 s, so 1/τ = 6.67 s⁻¹.
i(t) = 3 + (2 − 3) e<sup>−t/0.15</sup> = 3 − e<sup>−6.67t</sup> A. Forced part 3 A; natural part −e<sup>−6.67t</sup> A.
v<sub>L</sub> = L di/dt = 0.6 × 6.67 × e<sup>−6.67t</sup> = 4 e<sup>−6.67t</sup> V. Check at 0⁺: KVL gives 12 − 4 × 2 = 4 V. ✓
examples.answer: i(t) = 3 − e<sup>−6.67t</sup> A (forced 3 A, natural −e<sup>−6.67t</sup> A), v<sub>L</sub>(t) = 4e<sup>−6.67t</sup> V, and i = 2.9 A at t = 0.345 s.
examples.check:
import math
i0=12/6; iinf=12/4; tau=0.6/4
print(i0,iinf,tau,0.6*(iinf-i0)/tau, tau*math.log(10))

traps: Using the source value as the final value of every variable. In an RC step v<sub>C</sub> ends at V<sub>s</sub> but i<sub>C</sub> ends at 0; in an RL step i<sub>L</sub> ends at V<sub>s</sub>/R but v<sub>L</sub> ends at 0.
Putting x(0⁻) into the shortcut for a quantity that jumps at switching. Use x(0⁺); only v<sub>C</sub> and i<sub>L</sub> are guaranteed continuous.
Forgetting that τ uses the Thévenin resistance seen by C or L after switching, with sources killed.
Dropping the minus sign in the natural part. For a rising step x(0⁺) < x(∞), the natural term x(0⁺) − x(∞) is negative.
Treating a pulse as one step. A pulse has two switching instants; restart the formula at the second one.

quiz.q: State the continuity rule for capacitor voltage and inductor current at a switching instant.
quiz.a: Capacitor voltage cannot jump: v<sub>C</sub>(0⁺) = v<sub>C</sub>(0⁻). Inductor current cannot jump: i<sub>L</sub>(0⁺) = i<sub>L</sub>(0⁻).

quiz.q: Why does the natural part of a DC step response decay to zero while the forced part remains?
quiz.a: The natural part solves the source-free equation and has the form A e<sup>−t/τ</sup>, so it decays with τ. The forced part is the particular solution that follows the constant source, so it stays at x(∞).

quiz.q: R = 10 kΩ, C = 100 μF, V<sub>s</sub> = 5 V, capacitor uncharged. Find τ and v<sub>C</sub>(t).
L = 2 H, R = 10 Ω, V<sub>s</sub> = 20 V, i(0) = 0. Find τ, i(∞), and i(t).
quiz.a: τ = L/R = 0.2 s. i(∞) = V<sub>s</sub>/R = 2 A. i(t) = 2(1 − e<sup>−5t</sup>) A.

quiz.q: In the worked example, find i(0⁺) and i(∞). Why does one jump?
quiz.a: i(0⁺) = (10 − 0)/50 kΩ = 0.2 mA. i(∞) = 0 because the capacitor is open to DC. Capacitor current can jump because capacitor voltage cannot; the source suddenly fixes the resistor voltage at t = 0⁺.

quiz.q: Sketch v<sub>C</sub> when v<sub>C</sub>(0⁺) = 5 V, v<sub>C</sub>(∞) = 10 V, τ = 2 s. Give the initial slope and v<sub>C</sub> at t = 2 s.
quiz.a: The curve rises from 5 V to 10 V. Initial slope = (10 − 5)/2 = 2.5 V/s. v<sub>C</sub>(2) = 10 + (5 − 10)e<sup>−1</sup> = 8.16 V.

beyond: Not for the exam. Circuit simulators such as SPICE do not use this formula directly: their transient analysis steps through time with numerical integration rules (backward Euler, trapezoidal), and the exponential comes out as an approximation whose accuracy depends on the time step. The same first-order curve sets on-chip RC wire delay and the thermal rise of a power device. Search for Elmore delay, SPICE transient analysis and first-order thermal model.
